Newly hatched Magellanic rockcod larvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days] when reared at a stable temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. Upon eclosion, these yolk-sac larvae have a minute wet weight at birth of just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], reflecting the small diameter of the egg, which is roughly 0.8 mm across. This initial mass is far lower than that recorded for some other nototheniids, underscoring the particularly small starting size of this species. During the lecithotrophic phase, the alevin relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves to fuel development and early growth. The duration of this endotrophic stage is tightly coupled to water temperature, and under the controlled thermal regime described, the transition to first exogenous feeding occurs before the yolk is fully consumed. Field surveys suggest that the timing of this critical trophic switch may vary with local oceanographic conditions, but the laboratory-based estimate provides a robust benchmark for the species at 7.9 °C.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase and undergo larval metamorphosis, they grow rapidly while feeding on planktonic prey. Sexual maturity in females is attained at a total length of 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty for females of approximately 140 grams [Wwp = approximately 140 grams]. This body mass represents a substantial increase from the birth weight, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissue during the juvenile and sub-adult stages. The length-based estimate of 21 cm is consistent with the allometric growth patterns observed in related nototheniids from the Southern Ocean, where size at first maturation is often tied to local productivity regimes. After reaching puberty, individuals continue to grow, albeit at a slower rate, as energetic resources become increasingly directed toward reproductive functions. The ultimate total length that adult Magellanic rockcod can achieve is 43 cm [Li = 43 cm], a value that defines the species' maximum size under natural conditions.

Adult females exhibit a highly iteroparous reproductive strategy, producing a large number of small eggs during each spawning event. Field estimates indicate that a single female can produce approximately 70,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 70,000 eggs per spawning event] at 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], with spawning events occurring approximately 2.7 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.7 times per year]. This daily fecundity rate, when integrated over the entire spawning season, yields a substantial annual reproductive output. The underlying temperature of 7.9 °C is critical, as metabolic rates and gametogenic cycles in polar fish are highly sensitive to thermal conditions. Compared to other nototheniids, the maximum reproductive rate of Magellanic rockcod appears to be moderately high, likely an adaptation to the relatively productive coastal habitats it occupies around the southern tip of South America and the sub-Antarctic islands.

The lifespan of Magellanic rockcod has been estimated at 18 years [am = 18 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. This remarkable longevity is typical of many polar fish species, which often exhibit slow growth rates and extended lifespans as a consequence of the cold, stable thermal environment in which they live. The maximum recorded age of 18 years is derived from comparisons with the congeneric species Notothenia coriiceps, which shows similar life-history patterns under analogous thermal regimes. Such a long life allows for multiple reproductive events across the adult stage, contributing to population stability despite the relatively small size of the larvae at hatching. However, in the wild, the realized lifespan is likely shorter than the 18 years documented in the laboratory due to predation pressure, food limitation, and the energetic demands of spawning. Senescence eventually leads to a decline in physiological performance near the end of the lifespan.

Comparative studies of body size among nototheniids reveal that Magellanic rockcod occupies an intermediate position in terms of ultimate wet weight. The species attains an adult body mass of up to 1500 grams [Wwi = up to 1500 grams], placing it between the smaller cryopelagic species and the larger Antarctic toothfish. This ultimate wet weight is achieved after several years of sustained growth, during which the fish must balance the competing demands of somatic development and gonadal maturation. The allometric relationship between total length and body mass in this species is well described by a power function, and the value of 1500 grams at maximum size fits within the range predicted by such models for a fish of 43 cm [Li = 43 cm]. Furthermore, the total length at puberty for females of 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm] corresponds to a body mass of roughly 140 grams [Wwp = roughly 140 grams], confirming the tight coupling between length and weight during the juvenile-to-adult transition. These parameters collectively illustrate the life-history strategy of a slow-growing, long-lived polar teleost adapted to cold waters.
